Come Princely Oberon, I long to tast this Moly: pray bestow The Knight-hood of the Mellisonant Tingle tangle, Vpon our brother Mopsus, we will raise All of our house to honours. I alwaies thought I was borne to be a Queene. Am I deceiv'd and cheated, guld and foold? My lands, my livings, and my orchard gone? I am beholding to your liberality. I shall grow wiser.

And shee too Should dreame of Damon. — So, I am sure Still Cupids factor: well ere long I see There will be many an heire the more for mee. Another lover, Enamour'd of the Ground! Slid; I thinke he takes mee For Oberon already. Who, the madman? Every evening He walkes abroad into the vallie here With Thestylis. Farewell old walking Ivibush. Bold mortall, hold thy hand. Did we out of love And our intire affection, of all Orchards Chuse your's to make it happy by our dances, Light ayry measures, and fantastique rings! And you ingratefull mortall thus requites us. All for one Apple! You know, Iocastus, Our Grace have Orchards of our owne more precious Then mortals can have any: And we sent you A Present of them t'other day. I must confesse Their outside look'd something like yours indeed; But then the tast more relish'd of eternitie, The same with Nectar. They cannot speake this language, but in ours They thank you, and they say they will have none, They doe request you now To grant them leave to dance a Fayry ring About your servant, and for his offence Pinch him: doe you the while command the traitour Not dareto stirre, not once presume to mutter. Ti ti tatie. Our noble freind permits, Tititatie: Doe you not sir? Ti ti ta tie. Now begone. O good Mopsus! Good Mopsus but conceale us, And I will promise by to morrow night To get thee Thestylis. And I will. Well: We do •… . Nay be not so discourteous; Stay and take An apple first: you Iocalo give him one, And you another, and our Grace a third. Harke, Thestylis, the birds doe bid you joy. A beauteous Lady, bright, and rare, Queen Mab her selfe is not so faire. Yes beauteous virgin; Thy each part Has shot an arrow through my heart; Thy blazing eye, thy lip so thinne, Thy azure cheek, & christall chinne, Thy rainbow brow, with many a rose; Thy saphyre eares, and ruby nose, All wound my soule, O gentle be Or Lady you will ruin mee. How's this? are you no woman then? Can such bright beauty live with men? Indeed I thought no man but hee Could of such perfect beauty bee. I have an hearb, they Moly call, Can change thy shape (my sweet) and shall. To tast this Moly but agree, And thou shalt perfect woman bee. My Queene Iocasta thou shalt bee: Halfe your estate then give to mee, Else, you being gone, there none will be, Whose Orchard I dare here frequent. The other halfe let Mopsus take. Come let us walke, majestique Queene, Of Fairy mortalls to be seene. In chaires of Pearle thou plac't shalt bee, And Empresses shall envy thee, When they behold upon our throne Iocasta with her— Dorilas.

Pilumnus having lost this hopefull Sonne, Though he had two more children, fair Vrania And noble Damon; yet the death of Lalage Suffic'd not his revenge, but he a new implores His goddesse wrath 'gainst Claius: —Doth Ceres prize me thus? Shall Claius tread upon the flowry Plaine, And walke upon the Ashes of my boy? Will I be Archyflamen where the Gods Are so remisse? let wolves approach their shrines; Their howlings are as powerfull as the Praiers Of sad Pilumnus! —Such disgusts at last Awaken'd Ceres: with hollow murmuring noise Her Ompha like a thunder'gins to roare. (The Ompha if it menace speakes at large In copious language, but perplexed termes.) And laid this curse on all Trinacria. Sicilian swaines, ill luck shall long betide To every bridegroome, and to every bride: No sacrifice, no vow shall still mine Ire, Till Claius blood both quench and kindle fire. The wise shall misconceive me, and the wit Scornd, and neglected shall my meaning hit. Doe so then: For now you see with what unfortunate choice Pilumnus daughter, delicate Vrania loves The mad Amyntas: for the angry Goddesse, Though she repaid the wrong done to Philaebus, Yet not approving the reuengefull mind Of great Pilumnus, scourg'd him with his own asking, By threatning an unhappy marriage To his Vrania, unlesse he that wooes her Pay an impossible Dowry; for as others Give Portions with their daughters, Ceres Priests Vse to receive for theirs. The words are these, That which thou hast not, mayst not, canst not have Amyntas, is the Dowry that I crave ▪ Rest hopelesse in thy love, or else divine To give Vrania this, and she is thine: Which while the poore Amyntas would Interpret, He lost his wits. Take heed of love, Laurinda, You see th'unhappinesse of it in others; Let not experience in thy selfe instruct thee. Be wise my Girle: so come and follow me. How sweet a folly is this love? But rash youth, Alexis, (As youth is rash) runnes indiscreetly on While mature judgment ripened by experience Stayes for loves season. Yes, Alexis, Nothing's borne ripe, all things at first are greene, You are to hasty reapers that doe call For Sickles in the spring: Woemen indeed too soone begin their fall. Yet till curst Claius dye, as now he must, Alexis, and Laurinda, let my counsell Asswage the heat of youth; pray be perswaded A while for to deferre your nuptiall blisse; 'Tis but a while. Temper loves fire. Yet, loving paire, stay 'till a fayrer gale; He deserves shipwrack, ('tis the Marriners flout) And justly too, that in a storme sets out. Tis well; now let's goe take our place, to see For our sad griefes a sadder remedy.
He that's a womans keeper, should have eyes A hundred more then Argus, and his eares Double the number: Now the newes, what letters? What posy, ring or bracelet wooes to day? What Grove to night is conscious of your whispers? Come tell mee, for I know your trusty squire, Your litle closet blabbes into your eare Some secret, let me know it. Indeed I doe, Cupids a dangerous boy, and often wounds The wanton roving eye. So I would have thee, but not yet my Girle, Till loves prove happier, till the wretched Claius Hath satisfied the Gods. Hast thou not heard it? Tis impossible. Why I will tell thee, Thou knowest Pilumnus? Yes: This Pilumnus had a sonne Philaebus, Who was, while yet he was, the only joy The staffe and comfort of his fathers age, And might have still beene so, had not fond love Vndone him. Why thus; one Lalage, a beauteous Nymph As ever eye admired, Alphestus daughter, Was by her father promis'd him in marriage. But only promis'd: for the sheapherd Claius, (A name accursed in Sicilian fields!) Being rich, obtain'd the beauteous Lalage From sweet Philaebus: he sad heart being rob'd, Of all his comfort, having lost the beauty Which gave him life and motion; seeing Claius Injoy those lips, whose cherries were the food That nurs'd his soule, spent all his time in sorrow, In melancholy sighes and discontents; Look'd like a witherd tree oregrowne with mosse, His eyes were ever dropping Iceacles. Disdaine and sorrow made Pilumnus rage, And in this rage, he makes his moane to Ceres, ( Ceres most sacred of Sicilian powers;) And in those moanes he prosecutes revenge, And that revenge to fall on Lalage. Silly maid, His passions were not causelesse; and with what justice Could she deny Pilumnus? how oft hath he sprinkled, The finest flowre of wheat, and sweetest myrrhe Vpon her Altars! Lalage ru'd the time She flowted brave Philaebus. Now she was great With two sweet twins, the faire chast Amaryllis, And mad Amyntas; (an unlucky paire!) These shee brought forth, but never liv'd to see them: Lucina caus'd her sorrowes stop her breath. Leaving this matchlesse paire of beauteous infants, In whom till now she lives. Worse Then ever: Shee being dead whose life was his, Whose lookes did hold his eyes from shutting up, He pin'd away in sorrowes, griefe it was To see she was not his, but greater farre That she was not at all. Her Exequies being past, He casts him down upon that turfe of earth, Vnder whose roofe his Lalage was hous'd, And parlied with her ashes, 'till his own lampe Was quite extinguish'd with a fatall dampe. Here ended th'noble sheapheard. Why the Ompha, Having denounc'd against him, and he knowing The hate of old Pilumnus fled away, I think hee's sayl'd to the Antipodes. No tydings can be brought what ground receives him, Vnlesse Corymbus make a happy voyage; Corymbus that will search both East and Occident And when he finds him spill his captive blood. Which Ceres grant he may! Tender Laurinda Now dost thou see the reason of my care, And why my watchfull eyes so close observe Thy steps and actions.
Cruell Laurinda (if a word so foule Can have so faire a dwelling.) seale not up Thy eates, but let a pity enter there And find a passage to thy heart. And t'other, for old freindship Strangling his bitter Corrasive in his heart, Hath promis'd to desist from further suit. Then most unhappy me! And what I? Which hand am I? Then I am all despaire, no hope for me. Thy wife, Alexis? But how can it be Without a Husband? and I must be he. How without her heart? For that am I: besides you heard her say I was the right hand you the left, away, Desist Alexis, mine's the upper hand. But I am her desire, in that 'tis showne Her only wish is to make me her owne. 'Tis true, but I her fire. Yet when the flame is spent, The fire continues; Therefore me she meant. Alexis doe, so I her Maidenhead. Let's have another meeting, since her words Delude us thus, wee'le haue a pregnant signe To shew her mind. I'le the while retire Into the Temple, if I linger here I am afraid of meeting Amaryllis, Who with unwelcome love solicites me. Till then farewell. All but her to thee. The name of Rivall should not loose the Freind. Minds in love, Doe count their daies by minutes, measure howres By every sand that drops through the slow glasse; And for each vie a teare. Doe thou so too! Amaryllis, They cannot doe it: I have fixt my love So firme on my Laurinda, that for her I e're shall hate my selfe? For that I hate it! My Alexis Well met, I'ave been at your cottage to seeke you. Let us goe seeke her, To have a finall judgement. Content. Here comes my joy or death. But to me an Antidote. And me she slew to raise me up againe: You shall not slight us thus, what doe you thinke Of mee? Shew by some signe which of us You have design'd for happinesse. Now happy Damon shee thy Garland weares That holds thy heart chain'd in her golden haires! Tis more to take then give. By this your share's the lesse, you but receive. Then shee did approve Of my affection best, shee took my love. Then let our speares Plead for us, Yet tis, Alexis, clean against our oath. So neither shall enjoy her. So both should loose their hope! Laurinda, (The name which but to speak I would not wish For life or breath.) Let not thy powerfull beauty Torment us longer: Tell us which of us You value most. Or if he cannot so, as sure he cannot, Yet he will rather chuse to dye then live Once to oppose your liking. How, me Laurinda? That word doth relish immortalitie. Still more perplexed: what doe you think I am? Which I? Thus you scorne my love. Damon, desist thy suit or loose thy life; Thou heard'st Laurinda wish she were my wife. I am her head: That word doth seeme t'impart She meanes my marriage. But, Damon, I next to her heart doe stand: I am her hope, in that you plainly see The end of her intents doth aime at me. I am her flame. The flames the hotter, therefore her desire Most aimes at mee. She promis'd now I should injoy her Bed. I see she still conceales it, and with speeches Perplext and doubfull masks her secret thoughts. I goe that way a hunting, And will call for her. And would she might preuaile! All happinesse to Damon be Except Laurinda. Thus we in love and courtesie contend. I much wonder, Dorylas, Amyntas can be sad, having such follies To provoke mirth. But I am ne're at home; Thou and I, Damon, Are absent from our selves. That may end One of our miseries, and the others life! Now you are like cruell To both, and play the tyrant equally, On him you hate as much as him you love. O those words to me Are Poyson. And what am I? Most blessed I! this Garland once did twine About her head that now imbraces mine. But me she gave That which was hers. I think 'tis greater kindnesse to receive. I will dispute no more. And determine of our feares. Come Damon, by this argument let us prove, Which tis of us Laurinda best doth love. How early, Damon, doe lovers rise? He that of us shall have Laurinda, Damon, Will not be up so soone: ha! would you Damon? I much wonder the Sunne so soone can rise! No summer, Damon. And he doth rise From her to gaze on faire Laurinda's eyes. On whom depends our only happinesse. Yes, the first we meet. Devotion's not so early up as love. That modest rose He grafted there. The virgins now come from the Temple. That name breaths life & soul to poore Alexis. As many joyes crown mine With happinesse. No other blessing hath preserved mee. I'le instruct you, Take here the paper, pen and inke. You are to passe your censure, Being the first Nymph that we have met this morning, Which of us two must have the faire Laurinda.
